days.name: Monday · Phenomenon & Question
days.lesson: Begin with a real or modeled phenomenon connected to **Scientific Weather Observation**. Reliable meteorology begins with consistent, time-stamped measurements and clearly separated observations and interpretations.
days.lab: Design a standardized observation protocol and collect temperature, cloud, wind, pressure or forecast data at two times.
worksheet: State the phenomenon in neutral observational language before explaining it.

days.name: Tuesday · Measure & Analyze
days.lesson: Collect or interpret quantitative evidence using a consistent method. This week's main data skill is **measurement protocol**.

worksheet: Create a labeled table with units, time/location, and source.
Calculate or identify a change, range, average, rate, gradient, or category as appropriate.
Graph or map the evidence.
Write one pattern you can defend from the data.

days.name: Wednesday · Model the System
days.lesson: Develop or revise a model explaining the mechanism behind scientific weather observation. A model must show relationships, not just vocabulary.
days.lab: Construct a physical, diagrammatic, mathematical, or digital model of scientific weather observation and test it against the week's evidence.
worksheet: Use at least three terms accurately: observation, measurement, forecast, uncertainty.
Use arrows, vectors, contours, or energy/matter flows where appropriate.
State one assumption in the model.
State one limitation: what real atmospheric feature is simplified or missing?

days.name: Thursday · Forecast, Research & Source Check
days.lesson: Apply the concept to a real weather or Earth-system case using **Solanar Observatory** and, when appropriate, a primary official/scientific source.
days.lab: Use Solanar Observatory to locate a current or archived example. Save the location, date/time, source name, and the evidence you used.
worksheet: Classify each item you used as observation, forecast, official alert, model guidance, derived analysis, or background information.
Record one numerical or mapped piece of evidence.
Compare at least two sources or layers when possible.
State what remains uncertain or what additional evidence would improve confidence.
